tests.title: Unit 4: Supply and Market Equilibrium – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: Supply differs from stock in that supply is:
options: The quantity offered for sale at a given price and time
The total quantity available in the economy
questions.explanation: Stock is what exists; supply is the part offered for sale at a price.

questions.question_text: The supply function is written as:
options: Sx = f(Px, Pi, T, Tx, E, N)
questions.explanation: Supply depends on own price, input prices, technology, taxes, expectations and number of firms.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT a determinant of supply?
questions.explanation: Tastes of consumers affect demand.

questions.question_text: A rise in input prices will usually:
questions.explanation: Production becomes costlier and less profitable.

questions.question_text: Improved technology:
questions.explanation: Lower costs make firms willing to supply more at each price.

questions.question_text: A subsidy generally _____ supply, and a tax _____ supply:
questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers cost; a tax raises it.

questions.question_text: If producers expect future prices to rise, current supply will:
options: Fall as they hold back stock
questions.explanation: They withhold goods to sell later at higher prices.

questions.question_text: An increase in the number of firms leads to:
questions.explanation: Market supply is the sum of firms' supplies.

questions.question_text: Substitutes in production are goods:
options: Produced using the same resources, so more of one means less of the other (e.g., wheat and maize)
questions.explanation: A fall in the price of one may increase supply of the other.

questions.question_text: Natural factors affect the supply of agricultural goods because:
options: Output depends on weather and rainfall
questions.explanation: Good monsoon increases supply; drought reduces it.

questions.question_text: A supply schedule is:
options: A table of quantities supplied at various prices
questions.explanation: It is the tabular form of supply.

questions.question_text: If three firms supply 10, 20 and 30 units at a price, market supply at that price is:
questions.explanation: Add them: 10 + 20 + 30.

questions.question_text: Market supply differs from individual supply in that market supply is:
options: The sum of supplies of all firms
questions.explanation: Individual supply refers to a single firm.

questions.question_text: The Law of Supply states that, other things constant, as price rises:
questions.explanation: Price and quantity supplied are directly related.

questions.question_text: An assumption of the law of supply is:
options: Technology and input prices stay constant
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus applies.

questions.question_text: A schedule with price Rs. 5, 10, 15 and quantity 10, 20, 30 shows:
options: A direct relation between price and quantity supplied
questions.explanation: Higher price brings greater supply.

questions.question_text: The supply curve slopes upward because:
options: Higher prices give higher profits and incentive to supply more
questions.explanation: Producers supply more when it is more profitable.

questions.question_text: The law of increasing marginal cost explains the upward-sloping supply curve because:
options: Producing more raises MC, so firms need higher prices to supply more
questions.explanation: P = MC; rising MC means rising price for more output.

questions.question_text: Profit and entry of firms explain the upward slope because:
options: Higher prices attract new firms and encourage existing ones to expand
questions.explanation: Higher profits raise market supply.

questions.question_text: Which is an exception to the law of supply?
questions.explanation: Others: agricultural goods, perishable goods, expectation of price change, rare goods.

questions.question_text: Supply of agricultural goods is an exception because supply:
options: Depends on nature and the production period, not just current price
questions.explanation: Farmers cannot increase output quickly when prices rise.

questions.question_text: Supply of perishable goods is an exception because:
options: They must be sold quickly regardless of price
questions.explanation: Sellers cannot withhold stock.

questions.question_text: The backward-bending labour supply curve means that:
options: At very high wages, workers may prefer leisure and work fewer hours
Labour supply always rises with wages
questions.explanation: The income effect eventually outweighs the substitution effect.

questions.question_text: Expectation of a price rise can create an exception because sellers:
options: Withhold supply now to sell later at the higher price
questions.explanation: Current supply falls even as the price rises.

questions.question_text: Supply of rare goods (e.g., paintings of old masters) is perfectly inelastic because:
options: Their quantity is fixed and cannot be increased
questions.explanation: The vertical supply curve shows no response to price.

tests.title: Unit 4: Supply and Market Equilibrium – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: The market supply curve is obtained by:
options: Horizontal summation of individual supply curves
questions.explanation: Add quantities supplied by each firm at each price.

questions.question_text: In perfect competition, the firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of MC curve:
options: Above the minimum point of AVC
questions.explanation: A firm supplies only if price covers average variable cost.

questions.question_text: Expansion of supply means:
options: Rise in quantity supplied due to a rise in price
Fall in quantity due to a fall in price
questions.explanation: It is a movement up along the same supply curve.

questions.question_text: Contraction of supply means:
options: Fall in quantity supplied due to a fall in price
questions.explanation: It is a movement down along the supply curve.

questions.question_text: An increase in supply means:
options: Rightward shift of the supply curve
questions.explanation: More is supplied at each price.

questions.question_text: A decrease in supply means:
options: Leftward shift of the supply curve
questions.explanation: Less is supplied at each price.

questions.question_text: A change in quantity supplied is caused by a change in:
questions.explanation: A change in supply is caused by other factors.

questions.question_text: Which causes an increase in supply?
questions.explanation: Lower cost increases supply.

questions.question_text: Which causes a decrease in supply?
questions.explanation: Costlier inputs reduce supply.

questions.question_text: A subsidy shifts the supply curve:
questions.explanation: It reduces cost and increases supply.

questions.question_text: A tax shifts the supply curve:
questions.explanation: It raises cost and decreases supply.

questions.question_text: A rise in input prices shifts the supply curve:
questions.explanation: Supply decreases.

questions.question_text: A rise in the price of the good causes:
options: A movement along the supply curve
questions.explanation: It is expansion of supply.

questions.question_text: An improvement in technology causes:
options: A movement along the supply curve
A shift of the supply curve
questions.explanation: Supply increases.

questions.question_text: Market equilibrium occurs when:
questions.explanation: There is no tendency for price to change.

questions.question_text: Equilibrium price is the price at which:
questions.explanation: The quantity at that price is the equilibrium quantity.

questions.question_text: On a diagram, equilibrium is shown by:
options: The intersection of the demand and supply curves
questions.explanation: The point of intersection gives equilibrium price and quantity.

questions.question_text: At a price above equilibrium, there is:
questions.explanation: Sellers compete by cutting prices until the market clears.

questions.question_text: At a price below equilibrium, there is:
questions.explanation: Buyers bid prices up until the market clears.

questions.question_text: A stable equilibrium is one where:
options: After a disturbance, forces restore the original equilibrium
questions.explanation: In an unstable equilibrium, forces move price away.

questions.question_text: Adam Smith's "invisible hand" refers to:
options: The market mechanism guiding self-interested individuals to promote social good
questions.explanation: Individual self-interest leads to efficient allocation through prices.

questions.question_text: In a market economy, prices act as signals because:
options: They show scarcity and guide producers and consumers
questions.explanation: High prices signal scarcity; low prices signal abundance.

questions.question_text: A limitation of the price mechanism is that it:
options: Ignores equity and may not provide public goods
questions.explanation: It is efficient but may be unfair and fail for public goods.

questions.question_text: When demand increases (supply constant), equilibrium price and quantity:
questions.explanation: The demand curve shifts right along the supply curve.

questions.question_text: When demand decreases (supply constant), equilibrium price and quantity:
questions.explanation: The demand curve shifts left.

tests.title: Unit 4: Supply and Market Equilibrium – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: When supply increases (demand constant), equilibrium price _____ and quantity _____:
questions.explanation: The supply curve shifts right.

questions.question_text: When supply decreases (demand constant), equilibrium price _____ and quantity _____:
questions.explanation: The supply curve shifts left.

questions.question_text: When both demand and supply increase, equilibrium quantity:
options: Rises, and the effect on price depends on relative shifts
questions.explanation: Quantity definitely rises; price is indeterminate.

questions.question_text: When both demand and supply decrease, equilibrium quantity:
options: Falls, and the effect on price depends on relative shifts
questions.explanation: Quantity definitely falls; price is indeterminate.

questions.question_text: When demand increases and supply decreases, equilibrium price:
questions.explanation: Quantity change depends on relative shifts.

questions.question_text: When demand decreases and supply increases, equilibrium price:
questions.explanation: Quantity change depends on relative shifts.

questions.question_text: When demand and supply both increase by the same proportion, equilibrium price:
questions.explanation: Price stays the same but quantity increases.

questions.question_text: A rise in income, for a normal good, will:
options: Shift demand right, raising price and quantity
questions.explanation: Normal goods have positive income effects.

questions.question_text: A bumper harvest of wheat will:
questions.explanation: Greater supply leads to lower prices.

questions.question_text: A rise in wages in the car industry will:
options: Shift supply left, raising price and lowering quantity
questions.explanation: Higher costs reduce supply.

questions.question_text: A new technology in smartphone production will:
questions.explanation: Lower cost increases supply.

questions.question_text: A rise in the price of petrol on the car market will:
options: Decrease demand for cars, lowering price and quantity
questions.explanation: Petrol and cars are complements.

questions.question_text: A price ceiling is:
options: A legal maximum price, e.g., rent control
questions.explanation: It keeps price below the market level.

questions.question_text: A price floor is:
options: A legal minimum price, e.g., MSP or minimum wage
questions.explanation: It keeps price above the market level.

questions.question_text: A price ceiling set below the equilibrium price causes:
options: Excess demand (shortage), queues and black markets
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

questions.question_text: A price floor above the equilibrium price causes:
questions.explanation: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

questions.question_text: The Minimum Support Price (MSP) is:
options: A guaranteed price at which government buys crops from farmers
questions.explanation: It protects farmers from price falls.

questions.question_text: A black market arises when:
options: Price ceilings create shortages, so goods are sold illegally above the legal price
questions.explanation: Excess demand encourages illegal trading.

questions.question_text: Qd = 100 − 5P and Qs = 20 + 3P. Equilibrium price and quantity are:
questions.explanation: 100 − 5P = 20 + 3P gives P = 10 and Q = 50.

questions.question_text: Qd = 60 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 10. Equilibrium price and quantity are:
Qd = 200 − 10P and Qs = 50 + 5P. Equilibrium price and quantity are:
At price Rs. 10, Qd = 20 and Qs = 80. The market has:
questions.explanation: Qs − Qd = 60, so price will fall.

questions.question_text: At price Rs. 4, Qd = 70 and Qs = 30. The market has:
questions.explanation: Qd − Qs = 40, so price will rise.

questions.question_text: If demand rises by 20 units at every price, equilibrium price and quantity:
questions.explanation: The demand curve shifts right.

questions.question_text: Elasticity of supply is:
options: % change in price ÷ % change in quantity
% change in demand ÷ % change in income
% change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price
questions.explanation: Es = %ΔQs / %ΔP.

tests.title: Unit 4: Supply and Market Equilibrium – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: The five degrees of elasticity of supply are:
options: Perfectly elastic, elastic, unitary, inelastic, perfectly inelastic

questions.question_text: Perfectly elastic supply has Es equal to:
questions.explanation: The supply curve is horizontal.

questions.question_text: Perfectly inelastic supply has Es equal to:
questions.explanation: The supply curve is vertical.

questions.question_text: Unitary elastic supply means Es equals:
questions.explanation: % change in supply equals % change in price.

questions.question_text: For a straight-line supply curve, elasticity is determined by where the curve:
options: Cuts the axes (or passes through the origin)
questions.explanation: Origin gives Es = 1; X-axis gives Es < 1; Y-axis gives Es > 1.

questions.question_text: A straight-line supply curve through the origin has Es equal to:
questions.explanation: At every point, the ratio P/Q equals the slope, so Es = 1.

questions.question_text: A straight-line supply curve that cuts the X-axis has Es:
questions.explanation: The intercept on the X-axis makes the curve relatively inelastic.

questions.question_text: A straight-line supply curve that cuts the Y-axis has Es:
questions.explanation: The Y-intercept makes supply relatively elastic.

questions.question_text: Which affects elasticity of supply?
options: Time period and availability of inputs
questions.explanation: Others: nature of the good, storage and technology.

questions.question_text: With a longer time period, elasticity of supply:
questions.explanation: Producers can adjust output fully.

questions.question_text: Supply of perishable goods is inelastic because:
options: They cannot be stored or produced quickly
questions.explanation: Output cannot easily respond to price.

questions.question_text: Supply of manufactured goods is more elastic than that of agricultural goods because:
options: Output can be expanded quickly and stored
questions.explanation: Agriculture has a long production cycle.

questions.question_text: Price rises from Rs. 10 to Rs. 12; supply rises from 100 to 130. Es is:
Price rises from Rs. 20 to Rs. 22; supply rises from 50 to 52. Es is:
Price falls by 10% and supply falls by 20%. Es is:
By the arc method, P = 8 → 10, Q = 40 → 60 gives Es:
The point method of measuring elasticity of supply uses:
options: The ratio of price to quantity multiplied by the reciprocal of the slope
questions.explanation: Es = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q).

questions.question_text: Elasticity of supply helps the government in taxation because:
options: It shows how much of the tax producers can shift and the effect on output
questions.explanation: With inelastic supply, producers bear more of the tax.

questions.question_text: In agricultural price policy, elasticity of supply helps to:
options: Predict response of output to support prices
questions.explanation: Inelastic supply means a limited output response in the short run.

questions.question_text: Supply of land is perfectly inelastic because:
options: Land is a gift of nature and its total quantity is fixed
questions.explanation: Its total supply does not respond to price.

questions.question_text: Economic rent is:
options: Payment to a factor in excess of its transfer earnings
questions.explanation: It is a surplus earned by factors in inelastic supply.

questions.question_text: Agricultural prices are more volatile than industrial prices because:
options: Supply is inelastic and depends on weather while demand is also inelastic
questions.explanation: Small shifts cause large price changes.

questions.question_text: Elasticity of demand differs from elasticity of supply in that:
options: Demand responds to price inversely, supply directly
questions.explanation: Ed uses a downward-sloping curve; Es uses an upward-sloping one.

questions.question_text: When a sudden shortage occurs, the invisible hand:
options: Raises prices, discouraging demand and encouraging supply until equilibrium
questions.explanation: Higher prices ration the scarce good and attract more supply.

questions.question_text: The burden of a tax falls more on producers when supply is:
questions.explanation: Inelastic supply means producers cannot easily avoid or pass on the tax.
